title: Jingchen Zhu
text:
Yuyu Chen, Miguel Espinosa, Shuo Liu, and Jingchen Zhu
Presented on SMS 46th Annual Conference:
Strategic Human Capital IG&C Best Paper
Honorable Mention for Conference Best Paper Award
submitted to the Strategic Management Journal
Paper Slides


Abstract

Digital monitoring gives managers richer information, but its value depends on how managers deploy human capital. Using the staggered rollout of a tracking system in a large manufacturer, we show that monitoring raises total output by expanding span of control but does not improve average worker productivity. Productivity gains appear in teams led by managers with stronger task-allocation skill, who use the new information to deploy and retain high-performing workers more effectively. Monitoring therefore increases the returns to managerial resource-orchestration capability rather than substituting for it.

title: Jingchen Zhu
text:
Working Papers

Role-differentiated Learning within Organizations
Yuyu Chen, Miguel Espinosa, Yu Wang, Xinjue Yao, and Jingchen Zhu
Revise and Resubmit at the Strategic Management Journal
Paper


Abstract

Existing research has yet to reveal how learning is divided among members within organizational units. We develop a role-differentiated framework of learning in production teams, in which workers and managers develop distinct learning trajectories. Using detailed task-level records covering 79,639 products at a Chinese electrical-equipment manufacturer, we test the predictions of our framework. We find that workers’ experience significantly improves execution performance, whereas managers’ experience significantly improves coordination performance. Managers’ learning in coordination becomes stronger when they actively coordinate production by reordering tasks and reallocating workers. Worker and manager experience are also complementary, as accumulated worker experience strengthens managers’ ability to translate their own experience into shorter waiting time.

title: Jingchen Zhu
text:
Work in Progress

Attention by Algorithm: AI Screening, Accountability, and Expert Discretion
Yuyu Chen and Jingchen Zhu
We study the adoption of an AI-based disease-alert system at a large dairy producer. Using detailed cow-level diagnosis, treatment, and milking records, we examine how algorithmic screening reallocates veterinary teams’ attention and how this reallocation shapes the technology’s productivity effects. In particular, we find that AI alerts alter veterinarians’ incentives by making some cases more visible and their responses more accountable. Under capacity constraints, this heightened accountability can distort attention toward algorithmically flagged cases and crowd out veterinarians’ professional judgment.


Consumer Resources and Relational Contract: Evidence from a Livestreaming Platform
Yuyu Chen, Bo Hu, Qingxu Yang and Jingchen Zhu
This project studies how livestreaming agencies govern valuable consumer relationships when creators can move across organizations. Using proprietary data from a large international livestreaming platform, we track streaming activity, user viewing and spending, and changes in creator–agency affiliations. We examine whether audiences belong primarily to creators or agencies, whether agencies reduce customer losses by connecting valuable users to multiple creators, and whether access to agency-linked consumers serves as an informal incentive that rewards creator effort and encourages retention.


Worker Voice and Technology Adoption
Jing Cai, Yuyu Chen, and Jingchen Zhu
We conducted a field experiment with reinforcing steel workers across 11 projects operated by a construction company. Although adherence to quality standards is critical in the construction industry, worker compliance was limited. Neither monetary incentives nor informational interventions improved compliance. However, when workers were allowed to vote on the quality requirements that their own teams would be expected to meet, their quality performance improved significantly.

title: Jingchen Zhu (朱景琛)
text:
I am a PhD student in Economics from Guanghua School of Management, Peking University. I used to visit Harvard Center for International Development (HCID) in 2025 Fall semester. I am on the 2026–2027 academic job market.
My research lies at the intersection of organizational economics, behavioral economics, and political economy. I combine proprietary within-firm data, field experiments, and surveys to study digital transformation and AI adoption, particularly among firms in developing countries. I examine how digital and AI-enabled technologies affect firm performance and organizational outcomes, how they interact with traditional management practices, and what barriers firms face in adopting and effectively using them.
A central part of my research is conducted in collaboration with firms across a range of industries. So far, I have conducted research projects partnered with construction firms, manufacturing firms, diary farms, and online entertaining platforms.
A new strand of my research extends this firm-centered approach to questions in international trade and political economy. I have recently started some new projects studying how firms adapt their international operations and market strategies to an increasingly fragmented global environment.
